full_judgment:
Judge, Begumganj, Noakhali under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption of 36 decimals land as appended to the pre-emption petition. The petitioners' case, in a nutshell, is that the opposite party No.5, Sayed Noor Nabi in the pre-emption case having owned and possessed the case land appertaining to plot No.7981 transferred the same to pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 secretly by registered Kabala No.10466 dated 26.10.1997 which was registered on 03.12.1998. The pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 are neither co-sharer tenants of the holding nor contiguous land holders but they are mere stranger purchasers. Their further case is that the preemptors purchased 20 decimals land in plot No.7980 situated contiguous east to the case plot by registered Sale Deed No.10999 dated 07.12.1978 from Mohammad Ullah and others. The pre-emptors also purchased 131/3 decimal lands of plot No.7980 from the said Mohammad Ullah and others by registered Sale Deed No.10993 dated 08.12.1978. Thus, the preemptors became the owners of total 33'/2decimals land in plot No.7980. Again, they purchased TA decimals land of plot No.8354 situated contiguous north of the case plot from Lalmoti Begum by registered Sale Deed dated 12.01.1991. The vendee No.2 of the said deed is the wife of preemptor No.1 and is benamdar of him, thus she is impleaded as opposite party No.6. They are contiguous land holders of the disputed land. The case land being contiguous to their homestead is very essential for them. The pre-emtees-opposite parties No. 1-4 purchased the case land without any knowledge of the preemptors. They did never take over the possession of the case land. The preemptors came to know about the alleged sale deed in the last part of Falgoon 1405 B.S. while the pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 were filling up the lower part of the case land excavating soil from the nearby canal. Thereafter, on receipt of the certified copy of the alleged Kabala on 23.03.1999 the pre-emptors came to know about the alleged transfer properly and filed the present case. 

 5. The respondent No.1 was impleaded as opposite party No.23 in the Pre-emption Case. He filed an application on 24.06.1999 to be a co-preemptor under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act claiming that on 04.04.1999 summons was not served on him as per provision of Order V Rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial Court by order dated 24.06.1999 summarily rejected the said application with the observation that the date of knowledge had not been mentioned in the said application and the period of limitation for filing pre-emption case against the alleged sale deed also expired on 02.04.1999. 

 6. Subsequently, the opposite party No.23-respondent No. I filed another application on 07.07.1999 under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. He had been staying in Chattogram for long and he used to run a grocery shop there. After coming to visit his native's home at Noakhali on 20.06.1999 he came to know about the preemption proceeding and alleged transfer from his brother Nurul Huda, who is opposite party No.21 in the pre-emption case. He obtained the copy of pre-emption case or. 22.06.1999 and earlier he filed an application for adding him as co-preemptor on 24.06.1999 Within two months from the date of said knowledge. Since the date of his knowledge about the alleged transfer was not mentioned in the said application, the same was rejected on ground of limitation. The opposite party No.23 could not know about the alleged transfer due to the fraudulent activities of the opposite parties No.1-5. No summon had been served on the opposite party No.23 at all. According to law, the application for adding as co-preemptor must be filed within two months from the date of knowledge and accordingly the opposite party No.23 filed the said application within two months from the date of knowledge. The trial Court stated that the report of the process-server regarding summons was not found on the record. The opposite party No.23 prayed for review of the earlier order dated 24.06.1999 and to treat the application dated 07.07.1999 as one filed under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 13. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants and petitioners in Civil Appeal No.70 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021 and also on behalf of the respondents in Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 taking us through the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003 heard along with Civil Revision No.1302 of 2003, judgments and orders of the appellate Court below as well as the trial Court and other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon mis-reading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby mis-directed beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. The learned senior Counsel contends next that the High Court Division erred in law in not taking into account of the fact that the application of the co-preemptor was filed beyond the time prescribed under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. The learned senior Counsel contends next that the High Court Division committed error of law in not considering that from the evidence of the P.W.1, P.W.4 and 0.P.W.1 along with the certificate of the local Union Parishad (Exhibit-4) it is proved beyond doubt that summons in the Preemption Case was served on 04.04.1999. But the co-preemptor filed the application on 24.06.1999 which is not within two months from the service of summons on him, therefore, the application filed by the co-preemptor for adding him as co-preemptor is barred by limitation. The leaned senior Counsel submits lastly that the High Court Division committed error of law in reversing the judgment of the appellate Court below venturing into fresh assessment of evidence beyond its scope in revisional jurisdiction and failed to consider that on material issue both the Courts of facts concurred while disbelieving the co-pre-emptor's statement of knowledge within the purview of Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there-fore the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division warrants interference by this Division. 

 "The main contention in the appeal is that whether the claim of the co-petitioner Abul Kashem is barred under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and if the answer is "no" then whether the original pre-emptors' claim of pre-emption subsists as contiguous landholder inpresence of co-preemptor who appears to be a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding." 

 19. Prior to the amendment in the year 2006, Section 96(5) of . the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as SAT Act, 1950) provides for three types of persons for seeking pre-emption and lays down the order of priority among those three types. By referring Sub-section (5) of Section 96 this Division in the case of Md. Azimuddin Pramanik & others Vs. Sree Satya Narayan Pramanik & others, reported in 37 DLR(AD) (1985) 220 most candidly observed as follows: 

 20. It is palpably clear from the above that prior to the enactment of State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006 under Section 96 of SAT Act, 1950 the following categories of persons were entitled to claim pre-emption, viz. (i) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance and (ii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (iii) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. Among the afore-said three categories the first category always excludes the other two categories and in absence of the first category, the second category excludes the third category. 

 24. From the record, the preemptors appear to contend that the application filed by the opposite party No.23 for joining him as co-preemptor is barred by limitation. It transpires from the record that the co-preemptor filed an application on 24.061999 to join him as a preemptor, but the trial Court by order dated 24.06.1999 summarily rejected the said application with the observation that since the date of knowledge had not been mentioned in the said application the same was barred by limitation. Subsequently, the opposite party No.23 filed another application on 07.07.1999 for adding him as co-preemptor on the averment that, he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. He had been staying in Chattogram for long and he used to run a grocery shop there, but service of summon was made in his permanent address at Ekhlashpur village, Noakhali where he was not present at all at the relevant time. After coming to visit his native's home at Noakhali on 20.06.1999 he came to know about the pre-emption proceeding and alleged transfer from his brother Nurul Huda, who is opposite party No.21 in the pre-emption case and obtained the copy of pre-emption case on 22.06.1999. Earlier be filed an application for adding him as co-preemptor on 24.06.1999 within two months from the date of said knowledge. Since the date of his knowledge about the alleged transfer was not mentioned in the said application, the same was rejected on the ground of limitation. The opposite party No.23 could not know about the alleged transfer due to the fraudulent activities of the opposite parties No.1-5. No summons had been served on the opposite party No.23 at all. According to law the application for adding as co-preemptor must be filed within two months from the date of knowledge and accordingly the opposite party No.23 filed the said application within two months from the date of knowledge. The trial Court stated that the report of the process-server regarding summons was not found on the record. 

 26. Admittedly the preemptors, co-pre-emptor, preemptees and opposite parties No.18-24 reside permanently at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali district. O.P.W. 1 stated in his cross-examination that although co-preemptor runs his business in. Chattogram he resides permanently at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali. O.P.W.2 stated in his cross-examination that the co-preemptor resides in Chattogram in the pursuit of his business although his family live at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali and he comes to Ekhlashpur occasionally. 27. The co-preemptor deposed in the Court as witness No.1 on his behalf and he stated in the deposition that he is a businessperson having a grocery shop in Chattogram in the name and style 'Alamin Store' and he used to stay in Chattogram in the pursuit of his said business. In support of the aforesaid claim the co-preemptor filed Nationality Certificate dated 14.11.1994 and the Voter Identity Card (Exhibit-9). The Nationality Certificate was issued by Chattogram City Corporation while the Voter Identity Card was issued by the concerned Ward Commissioner of Chattogram City Corporation. It reveals from the Voter Identity Card that his profession was mentioned therein as business. Thus, it is evident that the co-preemptor runs business in Chattogram. Moreover, both the Exhibits-8 and 9 had been issued by the proper authority and the Nationality Certificate was issued on 14.11.1994 nearly five years before filing of the pre-emption case. Therefore, it cannot be presumed that the said Nationality Certificate was created and afterthought and had been procured fraudulently for the purpose of the pre-emption case. 

 28. The co-preemptor claims that he came to know about the alleged transfer on 20.06.1999 from his brother opposite party No.21 namely Nurul Huda. The co-preemptor as witness No.1 deposed sup-porting the said claim. The witness No.2 namely Abu Taber on behalf the co-pre-emptor deposed corroborating the co-pre-emptor i.e. witness No.1 in this regard. The witness No.2 categorically stated in his deposition that the opposite party No.21 disclosed about the alleged sale to the co-preemptor in his presence on 20.06.1999 at 5:00 p.m. Therefore, the co-preemptor has been able to prove the date of knowledge about the alleged transfer. But the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below most illegally found that without examining opposite party No.21 as to the date of knowledge, the co-pre-emptor failed to prove the date of knowledge. 

 33. In the light of the foregoing discussion and for the reasons stated above, the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1303 of 2003 warrants for interference by this Division and we find merit in the Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012. On the other hand, we do not find any merit in the Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021.
